notes.meaning: The chapter opens with a sad "but." Barnabas had just given the full price of his field (4:36-37). Ananias and his wife wanted the same praise. Like him, they sold some land. Their hearts were not really in it, though.

differ.view: Methodism's founding Bible notes say Ananias was surely not yet a true believer. All the believers were of one heart, so he was probably only planning to be baptized.
Calvin sees the couple as hypocrites. They were people who put on a show of faith that wasn't real, and Satan got into the church through them.

notes.meaning: With his wife's agreement, Ananias quietly kept some of the money. He laid the rest at the apostles' feet as if it were the whole price. Keeping money was not wrong in itself. Pretending that part was all of it was "an acted lie."

Peter could only have known about the trick because God's Spirit showed him. He says Satan, the father of lies, filled Ananias's heart. Even so, Ananias chose to go along with it. Lying to the apostles was really lying to the Holy Spirit, who was at work in them.

Nobody forced Ananias to sell. Even after the sale, the money was still his to use. He could have kept it all, or honestly given only part. His sin was the lie, not keeping the money. Peter says he lied "to the Holy Spirit" and then "to God." Many see this as showing that the Holy Spirit is God.

differ.view: Methodism's founding notes say every Christian who owned land did sell it then. Ananias's real freedom was in choosing whether to become a Christian at all.
Calvin teaches that no one was required to sell. He says those who claim believers may own nothing of their own have lost their wits.

notes.meaning: Ananias fell dead as soon as he heard Peter's words. This was God's judgment, not Peter's doing. God may have used the shock of being found out. The punishment was just. It was also kind in its way, because it warned others away from the same sin. Fear spread to everyone who heard.
Some younger men of the church wrapped his body and buried him. Quick burial was the usual custom. There was also no reason to wait, since it was plain that God had judged him.
About three hours later Sapphira came in. She didn't know her husband had died. Wesley calls those three hours a precious space: she had longer than her husband to turn back.

Peter named the amount and asked if that was the price. His question gave her a gentle chance to tell the truth and repent, which means to turn away from sin. She stuck to the lie. A half-truth told to fool people is still a lie.

To "test the Spirit" means acting as if God's Spirit could not see through their plan. The two had agreed together to deceive. Marriage, which should help each other toward good, became a partnership in wrong. Peter then tells her that she will share her husband's end.

She fell dead at once, right at Peter's feet, the place where the full gift should have been laid. The young men buried her beside her husband. The same sin met the same judgment. As for their eternal future, Matthew Henry says these secret things belong to God.

differ.view: If they were true Christians, they did not lose their salvation. Their punishment was for this life only.
We should stay silent beyond the judgment we can see. Ellicott compares 1 Corinthians 5:5, where the body is punished so the spirit may be saved.

notes.meaning: This is the first time Acts calls the believers "the church." A deep, holy fear came over them and over everyone who heard. God gave all ages a lesson: deal honestly with Him. Here God acted Himself. This does not give the church a pattern for punishing people this way.

After one miracle of judgment came many miracles of mercy, done by the apostles among the people. These answered the church's prayer in 4:30. The believers met together with one mind in Solomon's Colonnade, a covered porch in the temple courts.

After what happened to Ananias, many outsiders were afraid to join the believers lightly. This was especially true of the rich and powerful. Wesley takes it to mean that people who only wanted to look religious stayed away. Even so, ordinary people spoke highly of the believers.

The church still grew, and grew all the more. Many men and women were joined "to the Lord" Jesus himself. Luke takes care to mention the women. Keeping the church honest and pure did not shrink it. It made it stronger.

Many miracles were happening. So people laid their sick in the streets, hoping Peter's shadow might fall on them as he passed. Some commentators note that Luke doesn't say the shadow itself healed anyone, only that people hoped it would. Others think healing did follow, like the woman who touched Jesus' robe. Either way, the power was God's, not Peter's.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic writers have pointed to this verse in support of the healing power of saints' relics, which are bones or belongings of holy people. They reason that if a saint's shadow could heal, these things can too.

notes.meaning: Crowds came from towns around Jerusalem too. This is a first sign of the good news spreading outward. They brought the sick and those troubled by evil spirits, and every one was healed. The healings went on day after day.

The high priest and his friends were Sadducees, a Jewish party that denied the dead will rise. The apostles kept preaching Jesus' resurrection, and their success filled these leaders with angry, jealous zeal. This time they arrested all the apostles and put them in the public jail, hoping to stop and shame them.

That night an angel opened the jail doors and led them out. There is a touch of humor here, since the Sadducees didn't believe in angels. God freed them not to escape but to go right back to the temple and preach. He sent them to tell everyone the whole message of new, eternal life in Christ.

The apostles obeyed at once. At dawn they were teaching in the temple courts. Meanwhile the high priest called together the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council, along with the elders. He sent for prisoners who were no longer there. God was quietly making fools of their plans.
